questions.q: What was the immediate pretext Lord Dalhousie used to annex Awadh in 1856?
questions.a: Lord Dalhousie annexed Awadh in 1856 on the pretext of "misgovernment" by Nawab Wajid Ali Shah. A wrong answer (e.g., "Doctrine of Lapse" or "failure to pay subsidy") reveals confusion between Dalhousie's different annexation policies: Doctrine of Lapse applied to states without a natural heir (e.g., Satara, Jhansi), while Awadh was annexed for alleged administrative misrule despite having a recognized ruler.

questions.q: Explain how the Subsidiary Alliance (1801) weakened the Nawab of Awadh's control over the taluqdars before the 1856 annexation.
questions.a: The Subsidiary Alliance forced the Nawab to disband his army and accept British troops and a Resident at his court. Deprived of his own armed forces, the Nawab could no longer enforce revenue collection or discipline rebellious taluqdars, making him dependent on British support. A wrong answer that focuses only on the Nawab's loss of sovereignty without linking it to the taluqdars' growing autonomy misses the causal chain that made the 1856 Summary Settlement so disruptive — the taluqdars had already become accustomed to operating with limited Nawabi oversight.

questions.q: Using the NCERT data on village control (67% pre-annexation vs. 38% post-Summary Settlement), calculate the approximate percentage decline in taluqdar-held villages and explain why British officials believed this would benefit peasants.
questions.a: The decline is (67-38)/67 ≈ 43%. British officials believed removing taluqdars would allow direct settlement with "actual cultivators," reducing peasant exploitation and increasing state revenue. A wrong answer that only calculates the percentage without explaining the British rationale (or that claims peasants actually benefited) fails to grasp the gap between colonial policy intent and outcome — the NCERT explicitly states revenue demand rose 30-70% and peasants lost the taluqdars' flexible support during hardships.

questions.q: Compare Hanwant Singh's statement (Source 4) with the sepoy petition (Source 6). What common grievance links the taluqdar and the sepoy, and how does it reflect the wider social rupture caused by annexation?
questions.a: Both sources highlight the sudden, unjust seizure of hereditary rights: Hanwant Singh lost ancestral lands "at one blow" by British title investigations; sepoys saw their religious identity threatened by cartridges greased with cow/pig fat. The common grievance is the British disregard for established customs — whether land tenure or religious practice. A wrong answer that treats these as separate issues (land vs. religion) misses the NCERT's argument that annexation created a "chain of grievances" linking prince, taluqdar, peasant, and sepoy, all of whom experienced firangi raj as the destruction of their world.

questions.q: Evaluate the British claim that the Summary Settlement aimed to "reduce the level of exploitation of peasants while increasing revenue returns for the state." Use evidence from the NCERT text to support your judgment.
questions.a: The claim was not borne out in practice. While state revenue increased, peasant burden did not decline; revenue demand rose 30-70% in many areas, and the inflexible collection removed the taluqdars' traditional role as a buffer during crop failures or festivals. A wrong answer that accepts the British stated intention at face value ignores the NCERT's explicit assessment: "neither taluqdars nor peasants had any reasons to be happy with the annexation." This tests the historian's skill of comparing official rhetoric with ground-level outcomes.

questions.q: Construct a cause-effect diagram (in words) showing how the 1801 Subsidiary Alliance led to the 1856 annexation, which triggered the Summary Settlement, which in turn fueled the 1857 Awadh Revolt. Include at least four links in the chain.
questions.a: A strong answer will trace: (1) Subsidiary Alliance (1801) → Nawab disarmed, British troops stationed, Resident controls court → (2) Nawab loses authority over taluqdars → (3) Dalhousie eyes Awadh's resources ("cherry") → (4) Annexation (1856) on misgovernment pretext → (5) Summary Settlement removes taluqdars (67%→38% villages) → (6) Peasants face 30-70% higher revenue, no safety net → (7) Sepoys (recruited from Awadh villages) transmit rural anger to cantonments → (8) Taluqdars and peasants join 1857 revolt under Begum Hazrat Mahal. A weak answer lists events without causal connectors or omits the critical link between taluqdar dispossession and peasant overassessment.
